rows.definition: The line that holds two things in relation without making them one.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The line that holds two things in relation without making them one. Near enough to be reached, and never close enough to be merged.
rows.historical_meaning: Old Norse tjóðr (a rope for tying an animal within range), from Proto-Germanic *tauþra; a line that holds two things in relation without making them one was first a rope keeping an animal from wandering too far.

rows.definition: A field sized for more than a line. Space given so a longer answer is possible.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A field sized for more than a line. Space given so a longer answer becomes possible, rather than merely permitted.
rows.historical_meaning: A compound of text, Latin textus (a woven thing, a composition), and area, Latin area (an open space, a threshing floor); a field sized for more than a line gives a longer piece of writing the open ground it needs.

rows.definition: How a surface meets the touch — rough, smooth, woven, worn; the sensory channel of feel.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: How a surface meets the touch, rough, smooth, woven, worn. The sensory channel of feel, named from the same weaving that also names a written text.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin textura (a web, a weaving, a texture), from texere (to weave); how a surface meets the touch is named for the same weaving that gives text its own name.

rows.definition: The mark for a table header cell. A cut fragment as it appears in this library, not an English word.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The mark for a table header cell, kept in the Grammar exactly as this library cuts it rather than dressed up as an English word.

rows.definition: Compared with. The word that introduces the other side of a comparison.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Compared with. The word that introduces the other side of a comparison, once inseparable from the word for what came next in time.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English þanne (then, than), from the same Proto-Germanic demonstrative stem as that; comparison and sequence in time were not fully separated words until later English split them apart.

rows.definition: To acknowledge what another gave. Thanks names the giving so it does not pass unmarked.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Acknowledging what another gave. Thanks names the giving out loud, the same way the old word for gratitude was first simply a thought made spoken.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English þancian (to thank), from þanc (a thought, a favourable thought, gratitude); thanking was, at the root, thinking well of someone out loud rather than merely feeling it silently.

rows.definition: This particular one, already known to both parties. The word that says we mean a specific thing.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: This particular one, already known to both parties. The word that says a specific thing is meant, and not merely any thing of its kind.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English sē/þē, a demonstrative that later fixed into the definite article, from Proto-Germanic *sa; saying the has always meant pointing at a particular thing already known to speaker and hearer alike.

rows.definition: A place made for showing a made thing to those gathered to watch. The watching is part of the work.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A place made for showing a made thing to those gathered to watch. The watching is part of the work, exactly as the old Greek word for the place already implied.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek θέατρον (theatron, a place for viewing), from θεᾶσθαι (theasthai, to behold); a place made for showing a made thing has always been named for the watching that happens in it, not for what is shown.

rows.definition: A place made for showing a made thing to those gathered to see it. The watching is part of the work.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A place made for showing a made thing to those gathered to see it. The watching is part of the work, whichever of the two spellings is used.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek θέατρον (theatron, a place for viewing), from θεᾶσθαι (theasthai, to behold), via Latin theatrum and Old French theatre; the two modern spellings both name exactly the same place.

rows.definition: Belonging to performance before an audience. Of what is shaped by being watched.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Belonging to performance before an audience. Of what is shaped, deliberately, by the fact of being watched.
rows.historical_meaning: From theatre, Greek θέατρον (a place for viewing); belonging to performance before an audience is what shapes a thing theatrically, because being watched is never neutral to what is shown.

rows.definition: Organised by recurring meaning rather than by time or place. Of an ordering that follows what things are about.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: An arrangement that groups by what things are about rather than by when or where they occurred. Content sorted this way finds its neighbours through shared subject, never through a shared date.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek θεματικός (thematikos), from θέμα (thema, a thing laid down, a proposition), from τίθημι (tithenai, to place); organising by recurring meaning follows what a thing has been laid down as being about, not where or when it happened.

rows.definition: The recurring thing that gives a body of work its unity. Also the coherent set of surfaces a system wears.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The recurring thing that gives a body of work its unity, or the coherent set of surfaces a system wears. Both name what has been laid down as the subject.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek θέμα (thema, that which is laid down, a proposition), from τίθημι (tithenai, to place); the recurring thing that gives a body of work its unity is exactly what the Greek word first named, the thing set down as the subject.

rows.definition: The appearance of a god to a person — a showing, a manifestation made visible. Greek theophaneia, from theos (god) and phainein (to show). Not the god and not the belief: the moment the unseen takes a face.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The character-animator realm, where a puppet's face, eyes, mouth, hands and breath answer the camera in real time, taking on a life rather than only a shape. The showing the old Greek word named for a god's arrival among people is lent here to a puppet's — not the god, only the moment something unseen becomes visible.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek θεοφάνεια (theophaneia), from θεός (theos, god) + φαίνειν (phainein, to show); the moment the unseen takes a face, named for the showing itself rather than for the god or the belief around it.

rows.definition: The place that is not here — grammar's pointer to elsewhere, and the word that says a thing exists at all.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The place that is not here, grammar's pointer to elsewhere, and also the word that says a thing simply exists. Both point away from the speaker, toward what is merely so.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English þǣr (there, in that place), from the same Proto-Germanic demonstrative stem as the and that; grammar's pointer to elsewhere and the word that claims a thing exists at all share one old root for pointing away from here.

rows.definition: Of Thetis — sea-goddess and mother, who knew her son's fate and could not change it, in the Greek telling. A named power in this house's pantheon.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Of Thetis, sea-goddess and mother who knew what was coming and could not turn it aside. A named power in this house's pantheon, kept for what the telling carries.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek Θέτις (Thetis), of uncertain etymology, possibly kin to θετός (thetos, placed, appointed), though a pre-Greek origin cannot be ruled out.

rows.definition: How much substance a thing has across its narrowest dimension. What separates a line from a band.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: How much substance a thing has across its narrowest dimension. What separates a line from a band, measured rather than guessed.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English þicce (thick, dense, close-packed), from Proto-Germanic *thikkuz; how much substance a thing has across its narrowest dimension is the old sense of dense matter, measured rather than merely felt.

rows.definition: Of small extent across. Thinness lets light and pressure through that thickness would stop.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Narrow enough across that what a thicker barrier would block gets through anyway — light, pressure, a signal. Slightness here is a permission, not merely a measurement.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English þynne (thin, slender), from Proto-Germanic *thinniz, ultimately a Proto-Indo-European root for stretching; a thing made thin has, since the deepest root, been stretched rather than simply reduced.

rows.definition: Whatever can be pointed at and treated as one. The most general noun there is, which is why it is used when nothing narrower fits.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The word kept in reserve for whenever a narrower name will not fit. It promises almost nothing about what is named, only that it can be pointed at and counted as one.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English þing (a meeting, an assembly, and by extension the matter discussed there), from Proto-Germanic *thingam; the most general noun began as a specific gathering before it widened to cover whatever the gathering was about.

rows.definition: A single strand followed through a larger body. Also a line of conversation held across interruptions.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A single strand followed through a larger body, or a line of conversation held across interruptions. Both are the one twist that stays traceable through everything crossing it.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English þrǣd (a twisted thread, a filament), from Proto-Germanic *thrēdus, from a root meaning to twist; a line of conversation held across interruptions is named for the single strand followed through a much larger cloth.

rows.definition: The line at a doorway, and the level at which something changes. Both are places where crossing matters.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The point a value has to reach before whatever sits on the other side of it starts to happen. Nothing here changes gradually; it waits at the line and then simply occurs.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English þerscwold (a threshold), from þrescan (to thresh, to tread) with a second element no longer certain in sense; the line at a doorway was first the beam trodden underfoot when threshing grain.

rows.definition: To limit the rate at which something may proceed. Throttling protects what would break under the full flow.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Limiting the rate at which something may proceed. It protects what would otherwise break under the full flow, the way a narrowed throat holds back a flood.
rows.historical_meaning: Middle English throtelen (to strangle, to choke), from throte (throat), of Old English origin; limiting a rate keeps the old image of a passage narrowed at the neck so nothing can pass through it all at once.

rows.definition: From one side to the other of. Names passage rather than arrival.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: From one side to the other of. It names the passage rather than either the starting side or the arrival.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English þurh (through, throughout), from Proto-Germanic *thurh; the word has always named passage from one side to the other, never the arrival at either end.

rows.definition: How much passes through in a given time. Throughput and latency are different questions and are constantly confused.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: How much passes through in a given time. It answers a different question from latency, and the two are constantly mistaken for each other.
rows.historical_meaning: A compound of through, Old English þurh (through), and put, of uncertain further origin; how much passes through in a given time was coined to be measured against a separate question, latency, that is constantly confused with it.

rows.definition: A small preview standing for a larger thing. Also the digit that opposes, which is why it means a grip.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A small preview standing for a larger thing. Also the digit that opposes all the others, which is why the same word means a grip.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English þūma (thumb), from Proto-Germanic *thūmon-, from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning to swell; the digit was named for being the thick one, and its opposing grip is why a small preview borrowed its name.

rows.definition: One unit of a clock's counting. A tick is the smallest interval a system can tell apart.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: One unit of a clock's counting. The smallest interval a system can tell apart, named for the sound of the counting rather than for the time itself.
rows.historical_meaning: Middle Dutch ticken (to touch lightly, to tap), probably imitative of the light sound itself; a clock's smallest countable interval is named for the sound it makes rather than for the time it measures.

rows.definition: A record standing for a claim or a task. A ticket exists so nothing depends on someone remembering.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A record standing for a claim or a task. It exists precisely so that nothing depends on anyone remembering it unaided.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French estiquet (a small note affixed to something), from estiquer (to attach, to stick), of Germanic origin; a ticket has always been a small attached record standing in for a claim, so nothing depends on someone remembering.

rows.definition: One level in a stack of levels. A rank that exists only because there are others above or below it.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A place in an ordered stack, meaningful only in relation to what sits above and below it. Nothing is a tier by itself; the word names a position, not a property.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French tire (a row, a rank, a series), of origin not securely traced further back; one level in a stack of levels has always existed only in relation to the ranks above and below it.

rows.definition: Part of a named platform's name. A cut fragment as it appears in this library, not an English word.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Part of a named platform's name, cut here exactly as this library cuts it rather than treated as a word of its own.

rows.definition: The dimension along which things happen in order. What lets before and after be told apart.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The dimension along which things happen in order. What lets before and after ever be told apart from one another.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English tīma (a time, a period, a season), from Proto-Germanic *tīmon, kin to tide; the dimension along which things happen in order was named from the same root as the tide that reliably marks its passing.

rows.definition: A span between two moments, held as a value. Duration made arithmetic.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A span between two moments, held as a value that can be added and compared. Duration made arithmetic, borrowing the old mathematical mark for change.
rows.historical_meaning: A compound of time, Old English tīma, and delta, the Greek letter Δ long used in mathematics for a difference or change; a span between two moments held as a value takes its second half from the symbol for change itself.

rows.definition: Events laid along time's own axis, ordered as they happened. The record's spatial form — history you can walk.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Events laid along time's own axis, ordered exactly as they happened. The record's spatial form, a history a person can walk rather than only read.
rows.historical_meaning: A compound of time, Old English tīma, and line, Latin linea (a linen thread, a drawn line); events laid along time's own axis borrow the same idea of a line used to draw anything else in order.

rows.definition: A limit on how long a wait may last before giving up. A timeout is a decision about patience, made in advance.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A limit on how long a wait may last before giving up. A decision about patience, made in advance rather than in the moment of waiting.
rows.historical_meaning: A compound of time, Old English tīma, and out, Old English ūt; a limit on how long a wait may last is a decision about patience made in advance, before the waiting even begins.

rows.definition: A thing that counts a span and reports when it has passed. It watches so nothing else has to.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Something set to hold a span of attention so nothing else has to keep holding it. Its purpose ends the instant it reports that the span is over.
rows.historical_meaning: The agent noun of time, Old English tīma; a thing that counts a span and reports when it has passed does the watching so that nothing else in the system has to.

rows.definition: A mark saying exactly when. A timestamp is what turns an event into a datable fact.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A mark saying exactly when. What turns an event into a fact that can be dated and checked, rather than merely recalled.
rows.historical_meaning: A compound of time, Old English tīma, and stamp, Old English stempan (to pound, to press a mark); a mark saying exactly when turns a bare event into a fact that can be dated.

rows.definition: A small offered piece of help, and a sum given beyond what was owed. Both are given freely rather than required.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A small offered piece of help, and a sum given beyond what was owed. Both are given freely, in a sense the word's own murky origin has never settled.
rows.historical_meaning: English tip, in the sense of a small piece of help or a sum given beyond what is owed, entered as slang of obscure origin; the popular story that it stands for a phrase about insuring promptness is a later invention with no historical support.

rows.definition: The name given to a work, and the right of holding a thing. Both are claims made in public.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The name given to a work, and the right of holding a thing. Both are claims set down and made public, the way the old inscription always was.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin titulus (an inscription, a label, a superscription), via Old French title; the name given to a work and the legal right of holding a thing both descend from the same word for a claim set down in writing.

rows.definition: The handle of this house's second writer, whose poetry page carries it. A name rather than a concept.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The handle of this house's second writer, carried on their poetry page. A name, kept as given, and not expanded into more than it claims to be.

rows.definition: Toward a destination. The word that points a motion at its end.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Toward a destination. The word that points a motion at its end, and nothing else about it.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English tō (to, toward, at), from Proto-Germanic *to; the word has always pointed a motion at its end without saying anything about the motion itself.

rows.definition: A brief notice that appears, says one thing, and leaves on its own. It asks no answer and blocks nothing.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A brief notice that appears, says one thing, and leaves on its own. It asks no answer and blocks nothing, the way a toast is raised and then set back down.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin tostus (parched, roasted), the past participle of torrere (to burn, to scorch); a drink offered to someone's health took its name from spiced bread once floated in the cup, and a software notice later borrowed that same image of something raised for a moment and gone.

rows.definition: That which raises brief notices and lets them go on their own. Named for how the message pops up.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: That which raises brief notices and lets them go on their own. Named for how the message pops up, in the same gesture as the appliance rather than in any direct descent from it.
rows.historical_meaning: From toast, Latin tostus (parched, roasted); that which raises brief notices and lets them go on their own is named for the same popping-up image as the kitchen appliance, borrowed sideways rather than descended from it.

rows.definition: Two words run together in this library's own naming, not an English word. Flagged for the mis-cut band rather than defined.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Two words run together in this library's own naming, kept here as a flagged mis-cut rather than defined as a word of its own.
